_metadata.note: Historical examples are used carefully. Some entries explicitly identify an analogous public incident or a representative production pattern rather than claiming an exact trigger where a verified postmortem was not established.

scenarios.name: Node Crash
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. One VM or Kubernetes node stops responding. 2. Requests in flight on that node fail or time out. 3. Health checks remove the node from rotation. 4. A scheduler or auto-scaling group starts replacement capacity. 5. Stateless workloads recover quickly; local-only state is lost.
scenarios.userImpact: Some requests fail briefly or become slower. A resilient stateless API should recover with little visible impact.
cascadeEffects: Pods or processes on the node restart elsewhere
Queue messages being processed may be redelivered
A local cache becomes cold on replacement instances
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to a few minutes when health checks, node heartbeats, and error-rate alerts are configured.
recoverySteps: Remove the failed node from traffic
Investigate hardware, kernel, runtime, or capacity cause
scenarios.realWorldExample: Netflix popularized Chaos Monkey, which intentionally terminates compute instances to validate that services tolerate ordinary instance loss.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Start by saying an individual node failure should be a routine event. Explain statelessness, health checks, rescheduling, queue redelivery, and why local state changes the recovery story.

scenarios.name: Data Center or Availability-Zone Failure
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Power, cooling, network, or a shared facility dependency fails in one site. 2. Instances and zonal endpoints become unreachable. 3. Cross-zone load balancing shifts traffic. 4. Databases use replicas or failover mechanisms. 5. Capacity in surviving zones may become saturated.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see elevated latency, partial errors, or an outage if the system was concentrated in one zone.
cascadeEffects: Surviving zones receive sudden extra traffic
Queues and caches may lose zonal capacity
Recovery tooling may compete for constrained capacity
scenarios.detectionTime: Usually within minutes through synthetic checks, zonal health signals, and traffic shifts.
recoverySteps: Fail traffic away from the affected zone
Verify database writer and replica health
Increase or reserve capacity in surviving zones
Restore the zone gradually and rebalance
scenarios.realWorldExample: AWS publishes post-event summaries for regional and zonal service disruptions, including a Sydney Region event in June 2016, illustrating why applications should design across failure domains.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss whether the requirement is multi-zone or multi-region. Explain zonal dependency inventory, headroom, database behavior, and tested failover.

scenarios.name: Disk Full
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A filesystem approaches 100% utilization. 2. Databases, brokers, or log agents cannot append safely. 3. Writes slow down or fail. 4. Retries add pressure. 5. A node may become unhealthy or corrupt temporary work if safeguards are weak.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may be unable to create or update data. Reads may remain available until dependent processes crash.
cascadeEffects: Queue publishers blocked by unavailable broker storage
Automated recovery may fail because it also needs disk space
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes to hours depending on growth rate; alert well before exhaustion, commonly at multiple thresholds.
recoverySteps: Stop non-essential writes and noisy logging
Free safe-to-delete temporary data or expand storage
Restart affected processes only after write capacity is restored
preventionStrategies: Separate data, logs, and temporary files where appropriate
scenarios.realWorldExample: The GitLab 2017 database incident is a broader operational reminder that storage operations, backups, and recovery procedures require safeguards and rehearsal; a disk-full game day should validate those controls without claiming it was the exact trigger of that incident.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain thresholds, retention, emergency cleanup, integrity checks, and why deleting arbitrary files during an incident is dangerous.

scenarios.name: CPU Spike
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A code path, query, rule, or traffic pattern drives CPU toward saturation. 2. Request processing slows. 3. Queues grow and timeouts fire. 4. Retries amplify load. 5. Health checks may fail and remove capacity, worsening the spike.
scenarios.userImpact: Pages become slow, API calls time out, and some users receive errors.
cascadeEffects: Monitoring and debugging can become slower under load
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes through CPU, latency, saturation, and error-rate alerts.
recoverySteps: Rollback the triggering release or disable the expensive feature
Apply rate limits or shed load
Scale carefully if the workload can benefit
Profile the hot path after mitigation
preventionStrategies: Kill switches for expensive dynamic rules
scenarios.realWorldExample: Cloudflare's July 2, 2019 outage was caused by a WAF-related regular expression that backtracked enormously and exhausted CPU used for HTTP/HTTPS serving.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Connect CPU saturation to user latency and retry amplification. Mention rollback, load shedding, profiling, and progressive rollout.

scenarios.name: Memory Leak
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. An application retains objects that should be released. 2. Memory usage climbs over time. 3. Garbage collection becomes more frequent or expensive. 4. The process is killed by the runtime or operating system. 5. Restarts temporarily hide the issue before the cycle repeats.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see periodic latency spikes, failed requests, or reconnects as instances restart.
cascadeEffects: Replacement instances become overloaded while one restarts
Auto-scaling may add cost without fixing the leak
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes to days depending on leak rate; detect through memory trend, GC metrics, and restart frequency.
recoverySteps: Roll back recent changes if correlated
Capture heap profiles or dumps safely
Fix retention path and add regression tests
scenarios.realWorldExample: Many large platforms have published runtime memory regressions over time. Use this as an honest representative production failure pattern unless your course links to a specific verified postmortem.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Distinguish mitigation from cure: restarts recover capacity, while profiling and code changes remove the leak. Mention GC telemetry and canaries.

scenarios.name: Network Partition
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Two healthy groups of nodes cannot communicate reliably. 2. Each side has an incomplete view of the system. 3. Replication stalls or leadership changes. 4. The system must choose whether to reject operations, serve stale data, or accept conflicting writes. 5. Reconciliation starts after connectivity returns.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see stale reads, blocked writes, duplicate work, or region-specific behavior.
cascadeEffects: Retries cross healthy and unhealthy paths
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes with cross-zone probes, quorum alerts, and replication-lag monitoring.
recoverySteps: Preserve a single authoritative writer where required
Reconcile divergent state and audit data
scenarios.realWorldExample: GitHub's October 2018 incident included a network partition that affected database replication and required careful recovery, making it a useful public case study for failover safety.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss CAP behavior, quorum, fencing, stale leaders, reconciliation, and why browsing can remain available while risky writes pause.

scenarios.name: Packet Loss
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Some packets are dropped between clients, proxies, or services. 2. TCP retransmits and request latency rises. 3. Timeouts fire intermittently. 4. Clients retry. 5. Effective throughput falls even when bandwidth graphs appear normal.
scenarios.userImpact: Users experience sporadic slowness, failed uploads, audio/video glitches, or reconnects.
cascadeEffects: Tail latency worsens before average latency looks alarming
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes if monitoring includes retransmits, loss, tail latency, and synthetic tests from multiple locations.
recoverySteps: Reduce payload size or degrade quality
Tune timeouts only after understanding the path
scenarios.realWorldExample: Interactive communication and streaming platforms routinely design for lossy networks; adaptive bitrate and reconnect logic are practical responses even when a public outage report is not the source of the lesson.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain why packet loss is a tail-latency problem, not only a bandwidth problem. Mention retries, adaptive quality, and resumable transfer.

scenarios.name: Latency Spike
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A dependency responds more slowly than normal. 2. In-flight requests accumulate. 3. Worker threads, event-loop tasks, or connection pools fill. 4. Upstream timeouts and retries increase load. 5. The originally slow dependency receives even more pressure.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see slow pages, timeouts, and inconsistent success depending on the request path.
cascadeEffects: Autoscaling may amplify calls to the slow dependency
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes when p95 and p99 latency, pool wait time, and timeout rates are monitored.
recoverySteps: Investigate the dependency after stabilizing traffic
scenarios.realWorldExample: Large public incidents often show latency rising before errors dominate. Google SRE guidance emphasizes symptom-based alerting so teams react to user-visible degradation early.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Use this scenario to discuss tail latency, timeout budgets, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and graceful degradation.

scenarios.name: DNS Failure
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Authoritative DNS, resolver access, or routing to DNS servers fails. 2. Cached records continue working until TTL expiry. 3. New lookups fail. 4. Clients cannot locate endpoints even if servers are healthy. 5. Recovery may be slowed if internal tools depend on the same DNS path.
scenarios.userImpact: Users cannot open the application or experience partial failures as caches expire at different times.
cascadeEffects: Monitoring from some networks becomes blind
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes, depending on TTLs and resolver caches; synthetic resolution probes provide early evidence.
recoverySteps: Restore authoritative reachability or resolver path
preventionStrategies: Redundant DNS providers or resilient authoritative service
scenarios.realWorldExample: Meta's October 4, 2021 outage is a major example: backbone disruption caused DNS locations to withdraw BGP advertisements, making DNS servers unreachable even though they were still operational.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain that DNS is part of the production critical path. Discuss TTL trade-offs, authoritative redundancy, BGP reachability, and out-of-band access.

scenarios.name: TLS Certificate Expiry
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A certificate reaches its expiry time. 2. Clients reject the connection during TLS validation. 3. Health checks and internal service calls may fail. 4. Retries do not help. 5. Manual replacement becomes urgent if renewal automation did not work.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see browser security errors, failed API calls, or service-to-service outages.
cascadeEffects: Mobile clients may be harder to update if pinning is involved
Monitoring may fail if it uses the same endpoint
scenarios.detectionTime: Immediate at expiry, but prevention alerts should trigger weeks in advance.
recoverySteps: Issue and deploy a valid certificate
Verify full certificate chain and hostname coverage
preventionStrategies: Ownership for every certificate and domain
scenarios.realWorldExample: Expired certificates have caused widely visible SaaS outages, including a Microsoft Teams authentication issue reported in 2020. The enduring lesson is to automate renewal and alert before expiry.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Treat certificates as expiring production dependencies. Mention automation, monitoring, chain validation, pinning risks, and reload procedures.

scenarios.name: Traffic Surge 10x
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Legitimate demand rises tenfold. 2. Edge, application, cache, database, queue, and third-party limits are tested simultaneously. 3. Auto-scaling adds stateless capacity. 4. Shared dependencies saturate. 5. Users retry if the experience degrades.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see slow pages, rejected requests, unavailable inventory checks, or delayed background work.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes through request rate, saturation, queue age, and business-conversion monitoring.
scenarios.realWorldExample: Launches, sports events, and ticket sales repeatedly produce legitimate surges. AWS architecture guidance emphasizes auto-scaling and decoupled systems for resilient workloads.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Separate legitimate surge from attack traffic. Explain bottleneck sequence, admission control, queue buffering, and business-priority degradation.

scenarios.name: DDoS Flood
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Attackers generate traffic from many sources. 2. Network bandwidth, connection tables, WAF capacity, or application paths become saturated. 3. Origin servers and downstream stores receive pressure. 4. Legitimate requests compete with malicious traffic. 5. Emergency controls are applied.
scenarios.userImpact: Users cannot reach the service or experience severe latency and errors.
cascadeEffects: Alert floods obscure the primary signal
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes using edge telemetry, anomaly detection, and user-impact alerts.
recoverySteps: Protect origin access and preserve critical paths
scenarios.realWorldExample: Major edge providers publish DDoS trend reports and mitigation guidance. Use this scenario to teach layered defense rather than claiming application autoscaling alone can absorb a flood.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss volumetric versus application-layer attacks, edge filtering, origin protection, cost controls, and fail-safe degraded modes.

scenarios.name: Thundering Herd
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A popular cached item expires or a locked resource becomes available. 2. Many callers wake or miss simultaneously. 3. They all recompute or fetch the same data. 4. The source database or dependency becomes overloaded. 5. More requests time out and retry.
scenarios.userImpact: A popular page slows or fails exactly when demand is highest.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds through cache miss ratio, origin request rate, and key-level hotspot metrics.
scenarios.realWorldExample: Cache stampedes are a standard production failure mode across large web systems; Redis-oriented designs commonly include jitter and request coalescing to mitigate them.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain why cache expiry is a load event. Mention hot keys, jitter, stale serving, single flight, and source-of-truth protection.

scenarios.name: Retry Storm
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A dependency slows or fails. 2. Callers retry quickly. 3. Traffic multiplies beyond the original request rate. 4. The dependency has less opportunity to recover. 5. Upstream systems also time out and add their own retries.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see prolonged errors even after the original fault could have recovered.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes through retry counters, request amplification ratio, and dependency saturation.
scenarios.realWorldExample: Distributed outage reviews frequently show retries amplifying partial failure. Google SRE literature treats overload control and actionable monitoring as essential operational concerns.
scenarios.interviewAngle: State that retries are not free. Discuss idempotency, retry budgets, jitter, circuit breakers, and different handling for reads versus writes.

scenarios.name: Thread Pool Exhaustion
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Slow downstream calls occupy worker threads. 2. New requests wait for a thread. 3. Queue time grows. 4. Health checks may wait behind user traffic. 5. The service looks alive but cannot do useful work.
scenarios.userImpact: Requests hang or time out even if CPU usage is not high.
cascadeEffects: Load balancer may keep sending traffic
One dependency failure spreads to unrelated endpoints
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes using active-thread count, queue wait time, and endpoint latency.
recoverySteps: Apply bulkheads per dependency or endpoint
scenarios.realWorldExample: This is a common microservice outage pattern: latency in one downstream can consume every worker and spread failure. It is best taught as a representative mechanism unless a verified company postmortem is linked.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain why low CPU does not imply health. Discuss pool queues, bulkheads, timeout budgets, and separate health-check resources.

scenarios.name: Deadlock
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Two operations each hold a lock the other needs. 2. Progress stops until a detector aborts one operation or a timeout fires. 3. Clients retry. 4. Throughput falls and lock queues grow. 5. Repeated ordering patterns can recreate the deadlock.
scenarios.userImpact: Some updates fail or hang; users may see conflict errors or slow transactions.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes with deadlock logs, lock-wait metrics, and transaction latency alerts.
recoverySteps: Abort and retry safely with backoff
scenarios.realWorldExample: Relational databases routinely detect and abort deadlocks in production workloads. Treat this as an expected failure to handle, not an impossible edge case.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss database deadlock detection, idempotent retries, lock ordering, hot rows, and why longer transactions increase risk.

scenarios.name: GC Pause
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. The runtime pauses application work for garbage collection. 2. Request latency spikes. 3. Heartbeats and health checks may be delayed. 4. Upstreams retry or remove the instance. 5. Repeated pauses reduce effective capacity.
scenarios.userImpact: Users experience intermittent high latency or timeouts.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds when pause duration, p99 latency, heap occupancy, and GC metrics are captured.
recoverySteps: Tune heap and collector only after profiling
scenarios.realWorldExample: Large JVM-based systems have long treated GC pauses as a source of tail latency. The practical lesson is to observe pause time directly rather than infer it only from CPU.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Connect GC behavior to tail latency, heartbeats, and capacity. Explain profiling before tuning.

scenarios.name: Primary Database Failure
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. The database writer crashes or becomes unreachable. 2. Writes fail or block. 3. A failover controller evaluates replica health and lag. 4. A safe replica is promoted. 5. Applications reconnect and queued work resumes.
scenarios.userImpact: Writes fail temporarily; reads may continue if replicas remain healthy. Some recent writes may require reconciliation depending on replication mode.
cascadeEffects: Replica promotion may expose stale state
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes depending on health checks and guarded failover.
recoverySteps: Promote a verified replica or restore the writer
scenarios.realWorldExample: GitHub has published database-incident material that illustrates why promotion, replication lag, and recovery procedures require careful operational control.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss RPO, RTO, synchronous versus asynchronous replication, connection recovery, uncertain writes, and fencing the old primary.

scenarios.name: Replication Lag
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Replica apply rate falls behind the primary write rate. 2. Read replicas serve stale data. 3. Failover becomes riskier because the freshest replica may still be behind. 4. Backlog grows. 5. Storage or network constraints may worsen recovery time.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may not see recent updates or may receive inconsistent views across requests.
cascadeEffects: Replica storage grows due to retained logs
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes or faster with lag-in-seconds, log-position, and apply-rate monitoring.
recoverySteps: Delay promotion until risk is understood
scenarios.realWorldExample: Replication lag is a recurring issue in database incident reports, including public recovery discussions from large platforms such as GitHub.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain that read scaling introduces freshness decisions. Cover read-after-write routing, lag metrics, promotion safety, and product tolerance.

scenarios.name: Connection Pool Exhausted
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. All pooled connections are busy or broken. 2. New requests wait for a connection. 3. Latency rises and timeouts fire. 4. Retries add concurrency. 5. The database may also receive reconnection churn.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see slow or failed operations even if the database CPU is not fully saturated.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes using pool active count, wait time, timeout count, and database session metrics.
scenarios.realWorldExample: Serverless and rapidly autoscaled systems commonly expose connection-pool mistakes because compute can scale faster than a relational database accepts sessions.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Do the fleet-wide math. Explain pool wait metrics, long transactions, autoscaling interactions, and backpressure.

scenarios.name: Cache Miss Storm
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Cache entries disappear, expire together, or become unreachable. 2. Requests fall through to the source database. 3. Source latency rises. 4. More calls time out. 5. Cache refill slows and the outage sustains itself.
scenarios.userImpact: Popular pages or APIs become slow or unavailable.
cascadeEffects: Higher latency for uncached unrelated queries
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds through hit ratio, eviction, cache error rate, and origin-load dashboards.
scenarios.realWorldExample: Cache stampede and cold-cache events are common enough that major cache documentation and system-design guidance treat them as standard resilience concerns.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Differentiate a normal miss from a correlated miss storm. Explain stale serving, warming, single-flight, and source protection.

scenarios.name: Cache Eviction Pressure
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Cache memory reaches its limit. 2. Eviction removes keys according to policy. 3. Hit ratio drops. 4. Origin reads rise. 5. Hot data may churn if capacity or key design is poor.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see gradually increasing latency and possibly errors if the source database saturates.
cascadeEffects: Rate-limiter keys may disappear unexpectedly if mixed carelessly
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes to hours through memory, evictions/sec, hit ratio, and origin traffic.
recoverySteps: Increase capacity or reduce cached payloads
scenarios.realWorldExample: Redis operations guidance emphasizes monitoring latency and memory behavior because command mix, eviction, and resource pressure affect performance.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss cache classes, eviction policy, TTLs, memory economics, and why mixing sessions, rate limits, and disposable cache entries can be risky.

scenarios.name: Queue Full
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Producers create messages faster than consumers can process them or broker storage reaches a limit. 2. Queue depth rises. 3. Publish operations slow or reject work. 4. Disk and memory pressure increase. 5. Recovery takes time even after input drops.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see delayed work, rejected submissions, or stale processing status.
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes or sooner using queue depth, oldest-message age, publish failures, and broker storage metrics.
recoverySteps: Scale consumers only if downstream capacity permits
scenarios.realWorldExample: RabbitMQ documentation explains acknowledgement, prefetch, durability, and queue behavior because broker safety and consumer capacity must be designed together.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain queue as a buffer, not infinite storage. Mention oldest age, downstream capacity, admission control, and priority lanes.

scenarios.name: Consumer Lag
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Consumers process events slower than producers publish them. 2. Offsets fall behind. 3. Derived views, notifications, or analytics become stale. 4. Retention pressure grows. 5. Catch-up traffic can overload downstream systems.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see delayed notifications, stale feeds, or slow workflow completion.
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes using consumer lag, event age, processing rate, and error metrics.
recoverySteps: Find whether lag is caused by capacity, poison events, or dependency latency
scenarios.realWorldExample: Kafka-style systems make consumer lag a first-class operational signal because retention and replay decouple producer and consumer pace.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss partitions, consumer groups, lag in records versus time, catch-up safety, and why scaling consumers beyond partitions has limits.

scenarios.name: Poison Message
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. One malformed or unsupported message repeatedly fails processing. 2. The broker redelivers it. 3. The consumer fails again. 4. Healthy work may be blocked or repeatedly delayed. 5. Retry traffic hides the real issue.
scenarios.userImpact: Specific work remains incomplete; broader processing may slow if the poison item blocks a partition or queue.
cascadeEffects: Repeated external side effects if processing is not idempotent
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes through retry counters, repeated message IDs, DLQ metrics, and consumer error logs.
recoverySteps: Move the message to a DLQ or quarantine
scenarios.realWorldExample: RabbitMQ documents dead-letter concepts and acknowledgements because malformed or repeatedly rejected messages need a deliberate path.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Mention retry limit, quarantine, schema evolution, observability, and manual replay. Infinite retry is not resilience.

scenarios.name: Third-Party API Down
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. A vendor API returns errors or times out. 2. Application threads and connections wait. 3. Retries add pressure. 4. User flows that depend synchronously on the vendor degrade. 5. Background jobs accumulate.
scenarios.userImpact: Users see partial feature failure, delayed processing, or checkout problems depending on dependency criticality.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to minutes through dependency-specific latency, errors, and synthetic checks.
scenarios.realWorldExample: External-provider incidents affect even well-operated applications. Payment and email integrations commonly need retry, reconciliation, and degraded-mode planning.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Classify dependency criticality. Discuss timeout budgets, circuit breakers, async handoff, reconciliation, and whether a fallback is genuinely safe.

scenarios.name: Auth Service Down
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. The identity provider or token-introspection dependency becomes unavailable. 2. New logins and token refresh fail. 3. Existing sessions may continue if local validation is possible. 4. Services with synchronous auth dependency fail. 5. Emergency access becomes important.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may be unable to sign in or perform protected operations. Existing users may have partial access until tokens expire.
cascadeEffects: Support and admin tools may also fail
Recovery work may be blocked by the same identity dependency
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes through login success, token-refresh errors, and dependency checks.
recoverySteps: Preserve safe locally validated sessions where policy permits
preventionStrategies: Short-lived but locally verifiable tokens where appropriate
scenarios.realWorldExample: Meta's 2021 outage affected internal recovery access as network dependencies failed, illustrating why operational access paths must not depend entirely on the impaired production path.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss fail-open versus fail-closed by operation, token validation strategy, refresh behavior, and out-of-band recovery access.

scenarios.name: Configuration Drift
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Instances, regions, or environments no longer share the intended configuration. 2. Behavior differs unpredictably. 3. A deployment or failover exposes the mismatch. 4. Troubleshooting becomes difficult because code versions appear identical. 5. Manual fixes create further divergence.
scenarios.userImpact: Only some users or regions experience failures, making the incident confusing and intermittent.
scenarios.detectionTime: Hours unless configuration state is continuously compared and audited.
scenarios.realWorldExample: Cloudflare's November 18, 2025 outage was triggered by a database permission change that caused an oversized feature file to propagate across its network, illustrating the blast radius of configuration-driven systems.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Discuss versioned configuration, validation, staged rollout, kill switches, audit logs, and how configuration can be more dangerous than code.

scenarios.name: Clock Skew
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Node clocks diverge. 2. Token expiry, certificate checks, leases, ordering, and logs become inconsistent. 3. Some requests appear early or late. 4. Distributed traces become difficult to read. 5. Leadership or lock behavior may become unsafe in poorly designed systems.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see intermittent authentication failures, duplicate processing, or inconsistent timestamps.
cascadeEffects: Scheduled jobs run at wrong times
scenarios.detectionTime: Minutes to hours through NTP offset monitoring, authentication error patterns, and clock-health alerts.
preventionStrategies: Design ordering with logical sequence where needed
scenarios.realWorldExample: Clock skew is a classic distributed-systems failure mode even when it does not produce a famous public outage. It regularly appears in authentication, certificate, and lease troubleshooting.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Explain wall clock versus monotonic time, token leeway, logs, leases, and why distributed ordering should not rely only on timestamps.

scenarios.name: Split Brain
scenarios.whatHappens: 1. Network or failover mistakes allow two nodes to believe they are primary. 2. Both accept conflicting writes. 3. Data diverges. 4. Clients observe inconsistent state. 5. Recovery requires fencing one writer and reconciling changes.
scenarios.userImpact: Users may see lost updates, duplicate operations, or contradictory data. Financial and inventory impact can be severe.
scenarios.detectionTime: Seconds to hours depending on quorum controls and conflict monitoring.
scenarios.realWorldExample: GitHub's public database incident discussions are useful for understanding why failover safety, topology awareness, and cautious recovery matter during partitions.
scenarios.interviewAngle: Treat split brain as a correctness emergency. Discuss quorum, fencing, promotion rules, reconciliation, idempotency, and why availability should not override unsafe money-moving writes.
